paragraphs: Diffusion models generate data through a process connected to forward and backward stochastic differential equations. The choice of forward equation helps determine how that process behaves. This paper asks how to explore these choices systematically, given that successful hand-designed equations represent only part of the possible design space.

The authors propose a general framework for parameterizing diffusion models, with particular attention to the spatial component of the forward equation. Their construction uses symplectic and Riemannian geometry associated with the data manifold. The aim is to make properties of the data’s underlying geometry part of the mathematical design of the diffusion process.

The framework includes theoretical guarantees and connections to earlier diffusion models, placing existing approaches within a broader formalism. The authors also establish theoretical advantages from a variational optimization perspective and report experiments on synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR10 that support its effectiveness. The contribution is a principled way to develop diffusion processes beyond the particular forward equations already explored.
icml-2023-a-flexible-diffusion-model-66f.tldr: A geometry-based framework systematically expands how diffusion models’ forward processes can be designed.

paragraphs: Statistical whitening adjusts the relationships and variation in a population’s responses. It is useful in computational systems and may also matter in biological sensory processing. Existing circuit models achieve adaptive whitening by changing synaptic interactions, but the authors argue that these changes appear too slow and insufficiently reversible for the intended adaptation.

The proposed alternative changes individual neurons’ gains while keeping synaptic weights fixed. Starting from a new whitening objective, the authors derive an online algorithm that adjusts the individual variances of an overcomplete collection of projections. They then express this algorithm as a recurrent neural circuit containing interneurons that modulate gain.

Numerical results show that constraining the signs of the gains makes the circuit more robust to ill-conditioned inputs. An extension also produces a form of local whitening in convolutional neural populations, relevant to structures found in visual and auditory systems. These results provide a computational account of how gain modulation could support adaptive whitening, without establishing that biological circuits necessarily implement this particular mechanism.
icml-2023-adaptive-whitening-in-neural-p.tldr: A neural circuit model performs adaptive whitening by changing neuronal gains while keeping synaptic weights fixed.

paragraphs: Membership inference asks whether a particular example was used to train a model. This paper investigates that privacy risk for diffusion models. The authors find that attacks developed for GANs and variational autoencoders are largely ineffective here, because some require unavailable components and others rely on assumptions that do not fit diffusion models.

Their proposed attack, SecMI, queries the model and compares errors associated with estimating the forward-process posterior at individual timesteps. It follows the usual overfitting assumption behind membership inference: training examples tend to have smaller estimation errors than held-out examples. This makes the diffusion process’s own estimation behavior the evidence used to infer membership.

The experiments cover standard diffusion models, including DDPM, and text-to-image systems, including Latent Diffusion Models and Stable Diffusion. Across multiple datasets, the authors report precise membership inference with high confidence in both settings. The findings show that weak performance by attacks transferred from other model families does not establish privacy protection; an attack tailored to diffusion behavior can reveal training membership.
icml-2023-are-diffusion-models-vulnerabl.tldr: SecMI exploits timestep-level estimation errors to infer training membership in standard and text-to-image diffusion models.

paragraphs: Neural networks can learn to predict game-theoretic equilibria from representations of games. A common architectural choice is equivariance: when the game representation is permuted, the prediction changes correspondingly. This paper examines what that structural choice helps achieve and where it can restrict an equilibrium predictor.

The theoretical analysis covers approximators for Nash, correlated, and coarse correlated equilibria in normal-form games. The authors show generalization benefits for equivariant approximators compared with general ones. They also show that better approximation is possible when the distribution of game payoffs is permutation-invariant, so this additional advantage comes with an explicit condition on the games being modeled.

The analysis also identifies drawbacks involving equilibrium selection and social welfare. Predicting an equilibrium and choosing a socially desirable equilibrium are distinct concerns, and the architectural symmetry does not remove that distinction. Taken together, the results explain why equivariance can be a useful inductive bias while still limiting which equilibrium outcomes an approximator can favor. Its value therefore depends on the prediction objective and the payoff distribution.
icml-2023-are-equivariant-equilibrium-ap.tldr: Equivariant equilibrium predictors have theoretical generalization benefits but also limitations in equilibrium selection and social welfare.

paragraphs: Deep topic models learn layered document representations and hierarchies of meaningful topics. However, the authors identify a mismatch: these models commonly use a single-step generative process despite representing several levels of abstraction. They propose a progressive model that builds text observations through successive levels of detail.

The method first uses a knowledge-informed coarsening process to construct observations ranging from concrete to abstract. A corresponding generative model then moves in the opposite direction, gradually producing more concrete observations. A graph-enhanced decoder captures semantic relationships among words across the observation levels, incorporating those relationships into the progressive construction.

An information-theoretic analysis explains how the model can alleviate latent variable collapse, a problem in which latent variables fail to play their intended role. Experiments report improvements in the quality of both document representations and discovered topics. The significance is the alignment between a hierarchy of textual observations and a generative process that works through that hierarchy, supported by semantic relationships and a theoretical account of improved latent-variable use.
icml-2023-bayesian-progressive-deep-topi.tldr: A progressive topic model generates increasingly concrete text representations and can reduce latent variable collapse.

paragraphs: Self-supervised vision models are often compared through a single ImageNet linear-probing score. That score measures an outcome but offers limited insight into why a model succeeds or how to improve it. This paper develops an evaluation framework that separates prediction risk into several contributing sources of error.

The decomposition extends the classical distinction between approximation and estimation error. It contains four terms: approximation, representation usability, probe generalization, and encoder generalization. Separating these terms makes it possible to examine different aspects of the learned representation and the prediction procedure instead of attributing every score change to one undifferentiated measure of quality.

The authors provide efficient estimators for the terms and apply them to 169 self-supervised vision models, examining 30 design choices on ImageNet. Their analysis identifies major error sources and shows how improvements can involve trading one component against another. These tradeoffs differ between full-data and few-shot settings, making the framework useful for selecting or designing models around the amount of labeled data available.
icml-2023-evaluating-self-supervised-lea.tldr: A four-part risk decomposition explains self-supervised model performance and reveals tradeoffs hidden by a single probing score.

paragraphs: Excess risk measures how much a learned predictor’s error exceeds the reference level used in a learning analysis. Bounds on this quantity describe how effectively learning can improve as more data becomes available. This paper develops a systematic framework for deriving sharp bounds using offset Rademacher complexity.

A central feature is that the framework does not require the Bernstein condition. For some parametric and nonparametric supervised learning models, it recovers fast rates within one analytical approach while using minimal identifiability assumptions. The scope remains tied to those model settings and assumptions; dispensing with the Bernstein condition does not make the results assumption-free.

The framework also yields new results for least absolute deviations linear regression, including sparse regression, and improved results for deep logistic regression using ReLU networks. These applications connect the general theory to different forms of supervised prediction. The contribution is both a common route to previously established fast rates and additional guarantees for specific models, showing how one complexity-based analysis can support several learning problems.
icml-2023-fast-excess-risk-rates-via-off.tldr: Offset Rademacher complexity provides a unified route to fast excess-risk bounds without requiring the Bernstein condition.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to maintain a valuable selection of items when the available items keep changing. The objective is monotone and submodular, meaning that adding items does not reduce value and that additional items have diminishing returns. A matroid constraint specifies which selections are feasible.

The setting is fully dynamic: items can be inserted and deleted in real time. Both kinds of change matter because the algorithm must continue maintaining a useful solution as availability evolves. The authors introduce a randomized algorithm with a data structure designed to support these updates efficiently.

Their result combines a factor-four approximation with an amortized update time of approximately k squared, suppressing logarithmic factors, where k is the matroid’s rank. The approximation expresses a controlled gap from the best feasible value, while amortized time describes cost averaged across a sequence of updates. Together, these guarantees address solution quality and maintenance cost in the same framework, extending this classic selection problem to changing data.
icml-2023-fully-dynamic-submodular-maxim.tldr: A randomized algorithm maintains a factor-four approximation for submodular selection under matroid constraints as items arrive and disappear.

paragraphs: Fractal geometry offers tools for analyzing why neural networks generalize, but earlier approaches depend heavily on Lipschitz continuity. The authors explain that this assumption generally fails for neural networks and can leave the resulting bounds uninformative. Their goal is to preserve a geometric analysis without requiring that assumption.

They introduce a data-dependent fractal dimension through a classical covering argument from learning theory. The resulting generalization bounds apply to fixed or random hypothesis spaces and combine the new dimension with mutual-information terms. Thus, the analysis accounts for both geometric complexity and particular information relationships involving the learning problem.

To interpret the information terms, the authors develop a notion of geometric stability and connect their bounds to earlier work. They also establish a rigorous link with topological data analysis, enabling efficient numerical computation of the proposed dimension. Experiments across several settings support the theory. The contribution joins a less restrictive mathematical foundation with a way to estimate the geometric quantity that the bounds use.
icml-2023-generalization-bounds-using-da.tldr: Data-dependent fractal dimensions yield generalization bounds without Lipschitz assumptions and connect those bounds to computable geometric quantities.

paragraphs: Exploration becomes difficult when a reinforcement learning agent lacks frequent, informative rewards. Rewarding novelty can help, but in a large environment many new discoveries may have little relevance to later tasks. This paper uses knowledge acquired from text to guide exploration toward behaviors that are plausibly useful to people.

The method, ELLM, prompts a language model with a description of the agent’s current state. The language model suggests goals, and the agent receives rewards for achieving them. This turns the language model’s background knowledge into an exploration signal without requiring a human to supply goals during the process.

Evaluations in Crafter and the Housekeep robotic simulator show better coverage of common-sense behaviors during pretraining. On a range of downstream tasks, the pretrained agents usually match or improve performance. The result supports language-guided goal selection as a way to make exploration more purposeful, while the qualification matters: the reported downstream benefit is common across the evaluated tasks, rather than an improvement claimed for every task.
icml-2023-guiding-pretraining-in-reinfor.tldr: ELLM rewards agents for achieving language-model-suggested goals, improving meaningful exploration and usually helping downstream performance.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning depends on which examples are treated as positive and negative pairs. Data augmentation usually plays a central role in making that choice. This paper broadens the available guidance by incorporating prior knowledge from generative-model representations or weak attributes into the sampling of both kinds of examples.

The authors use kernel theory to construct a loss called decoupled uniformity. It supports the use of prior information and removes the coupling between positive and negative terms present in the original InfoNCE loss. They also connect contrastive learning to conditional mean embeddings, using that connection to derive tight bounds on downstream classification loss.

In unsupervised experiments, knowledge supplied by generative models improves learned representations for both natural and medical images. In the weakly supervised setting, the framework outperforms the unconditional and conditional contrastive approaches considered. These findings support treating prior knowledge as part of the learning objective and sampling process, giving contrastive learning a source of structure beyond the choices encoded by augmentation alone.
icml-2023-integrating-prior-knowledge-in.tldr: A kernel-based contrastive loss incorporates prior knowledge into sampling and improves representations in unsupervised and weakly supervised experiments.

paragraphs: Latent Gaussian process models help infer hidden state trajectories from sequences such as neural recordings. Their appeal is a principled description of how those trajectories vary over time. However, when the observation model is non-conjugate, exact posterior inference is intractable, and approximate methods can become expensive.

The proposed framework, cvHM, combines Hida-Matérn kernels with conjugate computation variational inference. It enables variational inference for latent neural trajectories in linear time and accommodates arbitrary likelihoods. Reparameterizing stationary kernels through Hida-Matérn Gaussian processes also connects two ways of specifying prior knowledge: dynamical-system assumptions and Gaussian-process assumptions about trajectories.

The implementation uses bidirectional information filtering, which the authors describe as more concise than earlier approaches. Hyperparameters are learned efficiently using the Whittle approximate likelihood. These components address both trajectory inference and model adjustment. The resulting contribution is an approximate inference framework that preserves flexible observation modeling while making the temporal computation scale linearly, with a mathematical bridge between dynamical and Gaussian-process descriptions of hidden states.
icml-2023-linear-time-gps-for-inferring-.tldr: cvHM combines Hida-Matérn Gaussian processes and variational inference to infer latent neural trajectories in linear time.

paragraphs: Finite observations leave multiple possible explanations for unseen situations. A learner’s inductive bias determines which explanations it favors. This paper treats that preference as a way to understand neural circuits: circuit features may become more interpretable when connected to the kinds of functions the circuit readily learns and generalizes.

The authors build a neural network tool that meta-learns functions a target circuit finds easy to generalize. Their central idea is that these functions reveal the explanations the circuit tends to choose when data are incomplete. This provides a practical route from a circuit’s learning behavior to its inductive bias, a relationship that is otherwise difficult to derive.

For linear and kernel regression, where the bias is analytically known, the tool recovers it. The authors also extract biases from other supervised learners, including spiking neural networks, and describe how the method could be applied to animals. An application to recent connectomic data illustrates the intended use: interpreting structural circuit features through the learning preferences they produce.
icml-2023-meta-learning-the-inductive-bi.tldr: A meta-learning tool reveals neural circuits’ inductive biases by identifying functions they find easy to generalize.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization often involves competing goals. A setting that improves one measure may make another worse, so a single objective may not capture what a practitioner wants. This paper addresses that issue for Population Based Training, an efficient hyperparameter optimization algorithm originally designed around one objective.

The authors introduce MO-PBT, a version of Population Based Training for multiple objectives. Its purpose is to extend that optimization approach to problems where several performance criteria matter together. The experimental settings examine precision versus recall, accuracy versus fairness, and accuracy versus adversarial robustness, covering different kinds of conflict that can arise when choosing a model.

Across the evaluated problems, the authors report that MO-PBT outperforms random search, single-objective Population Based Training, and MO-ASHA, a state-of-the-art multi-objective hyperparameter optimizer. These findings support extending Population Based Training to account explicitly for competing criteria. The evidence concerns the optimization problems studied; the contribution is an empirically successful multi-objective variant rather than a claim that conflicts between desirable properties disappear.
icml-2023-multi-objective-population-bas.tldr: MO-PBT extends Population Based Training to competing objectives and outperforms the compared optimizers on the evaluated problems.

paragraphs: Pure exploration focuses on identifying the best choice using as few observations as possible. This paper studies that goal across multiple related tasks: finding the best arm in linear bandits and finding the best policy in contextual linear bandits. The question is whether learning across tasks can reduce the observations needed overall.

The key assumption is that every task shares a common low-dimensional linear representation. The proposed algorithms, DouExpDes and C-DouExpDes, use double experimental designs to determine sample allocations for learning this shared representation. This makes the collection of observations serve a global learning objective that can benefit the individual identification problems.

The authors establish computational and sample efficiency and show substantially better sample complexity than solving each task independently. The gain comes from exploiting the assumed shared structure rather than repeatedly learning each task in isolation. The result demonstrates a theoretical benefit of representation learning in multi-task pure exploration, with the common low-dimensional representation providing the connection that makes this information sharing useful.
icml-2023-multi-task-representation-lear.tldr: Learning a shared low-dimensional representation reduces the samples needed to identify the best arms or policies across related bandit tasks.

paragraphs: Learning a distribution over functions means representing multiple plausible relationships, rather than producing only one prediction rule. Neural Diffusion Processes apply denoising diffusion to this task. They learn to generate function samples through finite marginals: joint distributions describing the function’s values at finite collections of inputs.

The architecture includes a custom attention block that incorporates properties of stochastic processes, including exchangeability. This makes the organization of the model reflect structural requirements of the function distribution it represents. The approach combines the flexibility of neural models for meta-learning with diffusion-based generation of possible functional behavior.

Empirically, the authors find that the learned distributions can closely resemble the true Bayesian posterior. They show that Neural Diffusion Processes can emulate Gaussian processes and outperform neural processes in their evaluations. The approach supports regression, implicit marginalization over hyperparameters, non-Gaussian posterior prediction, and global optimization. These results position it as a flexible way to represent uncertainty over functions, with posterior fidelity demonstrated empirically rather than asserted as an exact general guarantee.
icml-2023-neural-diffusion-processes-e07.tldr: Neural Diffusion Processes learn distributions over functions and empirically approximate Bayesian posterior behavior across several prediction and optimization tasks.

paragraphs: Sliced-Wasserstein Flow offers a nonparametric approach to generative modeling, but its adoption has been limited by generation quality and a lack of conditional modeling. This paper addresses both issues, seeking to make the approach useful when generation must reflect supplied conditions as well as when no condition is provided.

The conditional extension rests on an observation that, under certain conditions, flows for joint distributions coincide with those for conditional distributions. The authors use this relationship to develop Conditional Sliced-Wasserstein Flow. The qualification is part of the mathematical basis: the stated correspondence is conditional, rather than a universal identity for arbitrary distributions.

For image modeling, the authors introduce two techniques inspired by local connectivity and multiscale representations. These image-specific inductive biases substantially improve efficiency and generation quality. With the combined changes, the method achieves performance comparable to many deep parametric generative models on conditional and unconditional tasks. The findings demonstrate that a purely nonparametric approach can become competitive when its conditional formulation and image structure are handled together.
icml-2023-nonparametric-generative-model.tldr: Conditional Sliced-Wasserstein Flow combines conditional modeling and image-specific structure to improve nonparametric generation.

paragraphs: Gaussianization is a generative modeling approach that can be trained without backpropagation. It has performed well on low-dimensional data, but its convergence has been observed to slow as dimensionality grows. This paper investigates that scaling behavior for Gaussianization with random rotations, focusing on how many layers the method requires.

For Gaussian input, the authors analytically show that the required number of layers grows linearly with dimension. They argue that the slowdown arises because the model cannot adequately capture dependencies between dimensions. This explanation directs attention to relationships among coordinates as a source of difficulty when the input becomes larger.

Experiments with more general input distributions show the same linear increase in cost, although some distributions exhibit more favorable scaling. The analytical result therefore has a specific Gaussian-input scope, while the broader pattern is empirical and admits exceptions. The authors also investigate possible speedups and identify research challenges. Their contribution clarifies why success in low dimensions does not by itself settle how efficiently Gaussianization will scale.
icml-2023-on-the-convergence-rate-of-gau.tldr: Gaussianization with random rotations requires layers growing linearly with dimension for Gaussian input, with similar but nonuniform empirical scaling more broadly.

paragraphs: Multimodal learning can use information available within each modality and information that emerges only through interactions between modalities. This paper distinguishes these as uni-modal and paired features. The authors argue that benefiting from cross-modal interactions also requires adequately learning what each individual modality can contribute.

They identify insufficient uni-modal feature learning in existing supervised late-fusion approaches and prove that this deficiency harms generalization. Their proposed response is to choose between Uni-Modal Ensemble and a new method, Uni-Modal Teacher, according to the distribution of uni-modal and paired features in the task. The choice makes the feature structure relevant to how the model is trained.

Using a simple guiding strategy, the authors obtain results comparable to more complex late-fusion and intermediate-fusion methods across VGG-Sound, Kinetics-400, UCF101, and ModelNet40. The findings emphasize that a sophisticated fusion mechanism alone does not ensure strong representations. Preserving the information learnable from individual modalities, and matching the learning approach to the task’s feature distribution, can provide an effective route to multimodal performance.
icml-2023-on-uni-modal-feature-learning-.tldr: Task-guided selection between ensembling and uni-modal teaching addresses weak individual-modality learning in supervised multimodal models.

paragraphs: Learning to maximize a function becomes challenging when the function can have discontinuities. This paper studies one-sided Lipschitz functions, which satisfy the weaker requirement that growth is controlled in one direction. Pricing and contract design motivate the question of how much reward must be sacrificed while learning a maximizer.

The authors give an algorithm whose total regret grows as O(log log T), where T is the interaction horizon. Regret measures the accumulated shortfall associated with learning instead of already using an optimal choice. The bound has a universal constant independent of the function’s number of discontinuities or complexity, making that independence a central feature of the result.

A known lower bound establishes that the dependence on T is asymptotically optimal. Applying the algorithm, the authors obtain the same regret order for selling digital goods to multiple buyers and learning an optimal linear contract in a principal-agent setting. These results show that the specified one-sided regularity can support very low learning cost despite allowing more irregular functions than ordinary two-sided smoothness assumptions.
icml-2023-optimal-no-regret-learning-for.tldr: One-sided Lipschitz functions can be maximized with asymptotically optimal O(log log T) regret, with applications to pricing and contracts.

paragraphs: Applying language models to robotics requires connecting words with observations of the physical world. PaLM-E addresses this grounding problem by directly incorporating continuous sensor information into a language model. Its inputs interleave text with encodings of images and continuous state estimates, allowing these different forms of evidence to appear together.

The authors train the encodings end-to-end alongside a pretrained language model across several embodied tasks. These include sequential robotic manipulation planning, visual question answering, and captioning. The evaluations show that one model can handle varied embodied reasoning tasks across different observation modalities and multiple embodiments.

The model also exhibits positive transfer: joint training across large language, vision, and vision-language domains benefits its capabilities. The largest version contains 562 billion parameters and, alongside robotics training, achieves state-of-the-art OK-VQA performance as a vision-language generalist. The authors further report retention of general language capabilities with increasing scale. Together, the findings support integrating sensory grounding into a broadly capable language model through shared multimodal training.
icml-2023-palm-e-an-embodied-multimodal-.tldr: PaLM-E integrates sensor observations with language to support embodied reasoning and benefit from joint multimodal training.

paragraphs: Open quantum systems are commonly described using a density matrix, whose high dimensionality, complex values, normalization constraints, and dynamics complicate generative modeling. Q-Flow changes the representation of the problem so that standard deep generative models can be used more directly to study its evolution.

The authors reformulate the dynamics as a partial differential equation for the Husimi Q function, a corresponding probability distribution. They then represent this distribution using normalizing flows. To learn how the flow evolves under the high-dimensional equation, they develop methods based on the Euler method and the time-dependent variational principle.

The approach is demonstrated on simulations including a dissipative harmonic oscillator and a dissipative bosonic model. The authors report scalability and efficiency, with performance superior to conventional PDE solvers and state-of-the-art physics-informed neural network solvers, especially for high-dimensional systems. The contribution combines a probabilistic reformulation of quantum dynamics with techniques for evolving a generative model, connecting tools for probability distributions to a demanding class of physical simulations.
icml-2023-q-flow-generative-modeling-for.tldr: Q-Flow represents open quantum dynamics through probability distributions modeled by normalizing flows, improving the reported high-dimensional simulations.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can be interpreted as learning gradients of changing log-probability densities. This perspective supports guidance and suggests ways to combine existing models for compositional generation. The paper studies how to condition, modify, and reuse diffusion models, including why some compositions fail under current techniques.

For the failures investigated, the authors identify the sampler as the responsible component. They propose sampling methods inspired by Markov chain Monte Carlo that enable successful composition. This diagnosis matters because combining model information is only part of the generation procedure; the sampling process must also realize the intended combination.

The authors additionally propose an energy-based parameterization that supports new composition operators and more sophisticated samplers with Metropolis corrections. They report notable improvements across problems including classifier-guided ImageNet generation and compositional text-to-image generation. The contribution therefore links a diagnosis of sampling failure with changes to both sampling and model parameterization, expanding how diffusion models can be reused for controlled generation without treating every successful composition as a consequence of model combination alone.
icml-2023-reduce-reuse-recycle-compositi.tldr: MCMC-inspired samplers and an energy-based parameterization improve compositional generation with diffusion models.

paragraphs: Random walks can estimate quantities over a network by sampling its nodes. This paper modifies a given Markov chain so that its walker favors seldom-visited nodes and avoids repeatedly visited ones. The aim is more efficient sampling while retaining the target distribution associated with the original chain.

For a class of self-repellent walks controlled by a positive parameter alpha, the authors prove almost-sure convergence of the empirical distribution to the target. They also establish a central limit theorem and derive the exact asymptotic covariance. Increasing alpha reduces that covariance in the matrix ordering considered, giving a precise sense in which stronger repulsion improves long-run sampling precision.

For MCMC estimation, the asymptotic sampling variance decreases on the order of 1/alpha and approaches zero as alpha grows. This concerns asymptotic variance rather than zero error after finitely many samples. Simulations support the theory and explore increasing alpha over time, aiming to combine the empirically faster mixing seen at smaller alpha with the smaller asymptotic variance available at larger alpha.
icml-2023-self-repellent-random-walks-on.tldr: Self-repellent random walks preserve the target distribution while stronger repulsion provably reduces asymptotic sampling variance.

paragraphs: Ridge ensembles combine predictors trained on subsamples, creating two adjustable ingredients: the explicit ridge penalty and the subsample size. This paper examines how those ingredients jointly determine squared prediction risk. Its analysis uses proportional asymptotics, where feature count and sample count grow with their ratio approaching a constant.

The authors characterize combinations of penalty and limiting subsample aspect ratio that produce the same risk. From these equal-risk contours, they prove that an optimally chosen full ridgeless ensemble matches the risk of an optimal ridge predictor. Here, full means the ensemble is fitted over all possible subsamples, and ridgeless means its component fits use no explicit ridge penalty.

The paper also proves strong uniform consistency of generalized cross-validation across subsample sizes for estimating ensemble prediction risk. This supports tuning a full ridgeless ensemble without splitting the sample and yields a predictor matching optimal ridge risk in the studied regime. The findings clarify how subsampling and explicit penalization can achieve equivalent risk, while supplying a theoretical basis for choosing the subsample size.
icml-2023-subsample-ridge-ensembles-equi.tldr: In proportional asymptotics, optimally tuned full ridgeless ensembles match optimal ridge risk, and generalized cross-validation supports their tuning.
